discovery: Quantum cryptography: quantum key distribution and entanglement-based secure communication

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, USA

nominees.name: Artur Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: In 1984 Bennett and Brassard showed that the quantum properties of single photons (the no-cloning principle and the disturbance caused by measurement) allow two parties to establish a secret key whose security rests on the laws of physics, not on computational assumptions. In 1991 Ekert independently proposed a protocol in which security is certified by the violation of a Bell inequality, turning the foundational test of local realism into a practical resource. These ideas launched the field of quantum information and were rapidly demonstrated with photons in the laboratory, then over fibre networks and satellite links. They also led to device-independent cryptography, whose security follows from observed Bell violations alone. Quantum key distribution was the first clear example of the second quantum revolution: entanglement and single-particle control, once questions about the interpretation of quantum mechanics, became technology. Their work reshaped physics, cryptography and experimental quantum optics.
